newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan takes delivery of Mirage fighter jets.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan takes delivery of Mirage fighter jets.

text.p: Taiwan took delivery on Monday of the first batch of 60 Mirage 2000 fighter jets ordered from France to strengthen its air defences against rival China, the air force said in a statement.
"The Mirage warplanes purchased by the air force arrived in the evening," the air force said in a terse statement.
It did not say how many Mirages were received.

State-funded Central News Agency said five Mirage jets and associated equipment arrived in the island's eastern port of Hualien and would be sent to Hualien's Chia Shan military base for assembly at midnight.

"The air force will immediately start assembly and training ...so the Mirage fighter jets can undertake the task of safeguarding air defences in the Taiwan strait," the statement said. It gave no further details.
Taiwan's military took delivery of two U.S.-made F-16 warplanes in April.
Taiwan has said it needs the 60 Mirage and 150 F-16 fighters it bought in the early 1990s to counter a steady modernisation of China's three-million-strong People's Liberation Army.

China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, blasted the United States for selling the F-16s to Taiwan, saying the move had seriously harmed relations.
Beijing vows to retake the island eventually -- by force if necessary.
China mounted eight months of war games and missile tests near Taiwan in 1995 and 1996 in what it acknowledged was an attempt to dissuade the island from pursuing independence.
Under pressure from Beijing, Paris agreed in 1994 to halt all new arms sales to Taiwan, although it will complete delivery of the Mirage fighters ordered in 1992.

Taiwan's cabinet has proposed a 3.1-percent rise to T$260.2 billion (US$9.5 billion) in defence spending for fiscal 1997/98, which would represent one-fifth of the government's total budget of T$1.2435 trillion (US$45.22 billion).

In addition, the military has proposed a special T$47.4 billion (US$1.7 billion) budget for purchase of advanced French and U.S. warplanes. That budget would be part of a nine-year T$300.7 billion (US$11 billion) fighter procurement fund.
China vehemently opposes any military link between its allies and Taiwan, and it sees any sales of advanced foreign military technology to Taiwan as an encroachment on its sovereignty.
